{{Artificial intelligence}}
On 8 September 2026, [[artificial intelligence]] company [[OpenAI]] claimed a solution to the [[Navier–Stokes existence and smoothness]] problem with a [[smooth function|smooth]] external force.<ref name="KHbbc">{{cite news|last=Hays|first=Kali|url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cy7zygy3rl2o|title=OpenAI says it cracked 90-year-old maths problem in 88 hours|date=8 September 2026|work=[[BBC News]]|access-date=9 September 2026}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|last1=Sample|first1=Ian|last2=Milmo|first2=Dan|url=https://www.theguardian.com/science/2026/sep/08/openai-claims-to-have-solved-maths-problem-that-stumped-humans-for-decades|title=OpenAI claims to have solved maths problem that stumped humans for decades|date=8 September 2026|work=[[The Guardian]]|access-date=9 September 2026}}</ref> However, approximately 12 hours before OpenAI's announcement, mathematician Tristan Buckmaster made a statement on behalf of himself and partly [[Levent Alpöge]], claiming that their recent advances on [[Euler equations (fluid dynamics)|Euler equations]] (a special case of Navier Stokes), reported in the same post,<ref name="TBmastodon">{{cite web|last=Buckmaster|first=Tristan|url=https://mastodon.social/@tristanbuckmaster/117233413705701198|title=Today, Levent Alpöge and I have made public three results|work=[[Mastodon (social network)|Mastodon]]|date=8 September 2026|access-date=9 September 2026}}</ref> were leaked to OpenAI a few days earlier and may have inspired OpenAI's [[Prompt engineering|prompts for the agents]] in the process that led to the solution.<ref name="JKfortune"/><ref name="TBstatement">{{cite web|last=Buckmaster|first=Tristan|url=https://cims.nyu.edu/~tristanb/statement.pdf|title=Today, Levent Alpöge and I have made public three results|work=Buckmaster's departmental website at the [[Courant Institute School of Mathematics, Computing, and Data Science|Courant Institute]]|date=8 September 2026|access-date=9 September 2026}}</ref> OpenAI denied such direct use of their work, claiming "significant" differences in proof methods in the Euler case.<ref>{{cite news|last=Waldvogel|first=Miriam|url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/technology/2026/09/09/openai-claims-it-solved-elusive-math-problem-with-1-million-prize|title=OpenAI claims solution to one of math's $1 million Millennium Prize problems|newspaper=[[The Washington Post]]|date=8 September 2026|access-date=10 September 2026}}</ref><ref name="OAIpost"/>

Buckmaster made the statement after analysts tipped him and Alpöge that their "progress had been passed to OpenAI"<ref name="TBstatement"/>{{rp|2}} and intended to narrate the events from his perspective lest "a sequence of announcements say something [he knows] to be false".<ref name="GRusatoday"/><ref name="TBstatement"/>{{rp|4}} OpenAI researcher [[Sébastien Bubeck]] later posted on [[X (social network)|X]] disputing some of the claims thereof,<ref name="KNindiatoday"/><ref name="SBtweet">{{cite tweet|last=Bubeck|first=Sébastien|author-link=Sébastien Bubeck|user=SebastienBubeck|number=2097379411691516310|title=I would like to clarify a few things}}</ref> and the CEO of OpenAI [[Sam Altman]] retweeted Bubeck's statement and maintained that OpenAI had contacted Buckmaster and Alpöge in [[good faith]],<ref name="KNindiatoday">{{cite magazine|last=Nasir|first=Kazi|url=https://www.indiatoday.in/technology/features/story/explained-openai-solves-90-year-old-maths-problem-humans-could-not-so-why-is-everyone-angry-at-sam-altmanfe-2990761-2026-09-09|title=Explained: OpenAI solves 90-year-old maths problem humans could not, so why is everyone angry at Sam Altman|magazine=[[India Today]]|date=9 September 2026|access-date=10 September 2026}}</ref><ref name="SAtweet">{{cite tweet|last=Altman|first=Sam|author-link=Sam Altman|user=sama|number=2097385167002415140|title=I spent much of the weekend talking with the team who did this work}}</ref> while Buckmaster's statement highlighted some communication from OpenAI that could be seen as hostile.<ref name="RBtc">{{cite news|last=Brandom|first=Russell|url=https://techcrunch.com/2026/09/08/openai-fought-dirty-on-career-making-math-problem-says-nyu-mathematician|title=OpenAI fought dirty on career-making math problem, says NYU mathematician|work=[[TechCrunch]]|date=8 September 2026|access-date=9 September 2026}}</ref><ref name="JKfortune">{{cite magazine|last=Kahn|first=Jeremy|url=https://fortune.com/2026/09/08/openai-says-it-cracked-navier-stokes-math-grand-challenge-buckmaster-accusation-cheating-intimidation-tao-lament|title=OpenAI says it cracked one of math's grand challenges. But there are troubling questions about how they did it—and what it means for us all|magazine=[[Fortune (magazine)|Fortune]]|date=8 September 2026|access-date=9 September 2026}}</ref><ref name="RHverge"/><ref name="TBstatement"/>{{rp|3}} Buckmaster also raised concerns about whether OpenAI could have accessed user data from [[OpenAI Codex (AI agent)|Codex]], an AI agent developed by OpenAI which Buckmaster and Alpöge used during their research, either directly or as anonymised [[training data]].<ref name="MMaxios">{{cite news|last=Mills|first=Madison|url=https://www.axios.com/2026/09/08/openai-math-solution-navier-stokes-credit|title=OpenAI's historic math solution overshadowed by credit controversy|work=[[Axios (website)|Axios]]|date=8 September 2026|access-date=9 September 2026}}</ref><ref name="MMTPMWsz"/>

The [[Clay Mathematics Institute]] listed solving one of four instances of the Navier–Stokes existence and smoothness problem as one of the [[Millennium Prize Problems]] and pledged to pay US$1 million for a solution to each.<ref>{{cite book|year=2006|editor1-last=Carlson|editor1-first=James|editor2-last=Jaffe|editor2-first=Arthur|editor3-last=Wiles|editor3-first=Andrew|editor3-link=Andrew Wiles|title=The Millennium Prize Problems|location=Providence, RI|publisher=American Mathematical Society and Clay Mathematics Institute|isbn=978-0-8218-3679-8|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131020203334/http://www.claymath.org/library/monographs/MPP.pdf|archive-date=20 October 2013|url=http://www.claymath.org/library/monographs/MPP.pdf|access-date=9 September 2026}}</ref>{{efn|The only time this pledge was invoked was in 2010 when [[Grigori Perelman]]'s proof of the [[Poincaré conjecture]] was accepted, but Perelman rejected the prize, considering previous work of [[Richard S. Hamilton]] more fundamental and hence making the latter more entitled to the award.<ref>{{cite web|title=Russian mathematician rejects $1 million prize|url=http://www.physorg.com/news197209671.html|agency=[[Associated Press]]|via=[[PhysOrg]]|first=Malcolm|last=Ritter|date=1 July 2010|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120117202129/http://www.physorg.com/news197209671.html|archive-date=17 January 2012|access-date=9 September 2026}}</ref>}} The Buckmaster statement and the OpenAI announcement both confirm that OpenAI does not plan to claim the award, and the Institute has yet to acknowledge any party for a correct solution. Some observers have seen the controversy as part of [[competition in artificial intelligence]], questioning the role of Alpöge's employment by rival AI company [[Anthropic]]; OpenAI stated they began large-scale work on all Millennium Prize Problems on 1 September, following rumours that Anthropic had solved two such problems.<ref name="DCnature"/><ref name="CZACscience">{{cite news|last1=Zhao|first1=Celina|last2=Cho|first2=Adrian|url=https://www.science.org/content/article/how-ai-math-breakthrough-ignited-controversy|title=How an AI math breakthrough ignited a controversy|work=[[Science (journal)|Science]]|date=8 September 2026|access-date=9 September 2026}}</ref><ref name="MMaxios"/><ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.economist.com/science-and-technology/2026/09/09/openais-apparent-maths-breakthrough-raises-profound-questions|title=OpenAI's apparent maths breakthrough raises profound questions|newspaper=[[The Economist]]|date=9 September 2026|access-date=10 September 2026}}</ref><ref name="RHverge"/> A declaration published on 11 September and signed by 26 [[Fields Medal|Fields Medalists]], titled A Severe Misalignment of AI in Mathematics, warned against "detrimental" impact on mathematics from AI companies treating unsolved problems as [[Language model benchmark|benchmarks]] without enhancing human understanding.<ref name="economist11">{{cite news|url=https://www.economist.com/science-and-technology/2026/09/11/top-mathematicians-are-outraged-by-openais-methods|title=Top mathematicians are outraged by OpenAI's methods|newspaper=[[The Economist]]|date=11 September 2026|access-date=19 September 2026}}</ref><ref name="fieldsOpenLetter">{{cite document|title=A Severe Misalignment of AI in == Background ==
=== Work before Buckmaster and Alpöge ===
{{main|Navier–Stokes existence and smoothness|Euler equations (fluid dynamics)}}
The [[Navier–Stokes equations]] are a system of [[partial differential equation]]s that has the [[Fluid dynamics|physical interpretation]] of describing the velocity and pressure of certain [[fluid]]s in space, potentially in the presence of an external force (e.g. gravity). The [[Euler equations (fluid dynamics)|Euler equations]] are a special case of Navier–Stokes equations where the [[viscosity]] of the fluid is zero, a property called [[superfluidity]].<ref name="CFps">{{cite web|last=Fefferman|first=Charles|author-link=Charles Fefferman|url=https://www.claymath.org/wp-content/uploads/2022/06/navierstokes.pdf|date=June 2022|title=Existence and smoothness of the Navier–Stokes equation|access-date=9 September 2026}}</ref>{{rp|1}} The [[Navier–Stokes existence and smoothness]] problem asks specifically whether "physically reasonable solutions exist" for these equations in the case where the fluid is [[Incompressible flow|incompressible]], does not have superfluidity (i.e. the viscosity is positive), the space is [[Three-dimensional space|three-dimensional Euclidean]], the initial condition is [[Smoothness|smooth]], and with an external force. There are different variations of the Navier–Stokes existence and smoothness problem, depending on whether the external force is smooth or equal to zero. Here, "physically reasonable" entails that the solutions are also smooth, globally defined, and that their [[kinetic energy]] is globally bounded. [[Charles Fefferman]]'s problem statement for the [[Clay Mathematics Institute]]'s [[Millennium Prize Problems]] asks to prove one of four statements, where the first pair (A) and (B) correspond to a positive answer to the question ("existence and smoothness") in the absence of an external force, and the last pair (C) and (D) to a negative answer to the question ("breakdown") in the presence of a [[smooth function|smooth]] external force. Each pair is in two different settings of the space being unbounded or periodic.<ref name="CFps"/>{{rp|2}}

In 2013, Guo Luo and [[Thomas Hou]] presented numerical evidence that solutions to Euler equations could reach a blowup [[Singularity (mathematics)|singularity]] in finite time, tilting public opinion about the answer to the Navier–Stokes problem.<ref>{{cite magazine|last=Kakaes|first=Konstantin|url=https://www.quantamagazine.org/ai-has-solved-one-of-maths-1-million-millennium-prize-problems-20260908|title=AI Has Solved One of Math's $1 Million Millennium Prize Problems|magazine=[[Quanta Magazine]]|date=8 September 2026|access-date=9 September 2026}}</ref><ref name="MMTPMWsz"/><ref>{{cite journal|last1=Luo|first1=Guo|last2=Hou|first2=Thomas|author-link2=Thomas Hou|title=Potentially singular solutions of the 3D axisymmetric Euler equations|journal=[[Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America]]|volume=111|number=36|pages=12968–12973|year=2014|orig-date=1 October 2013|doi=10.1073/pnas.1405238111 |doi-access=free |pmid=25157172 |pmc=4246962 |arxiv=1310.0497 |bibcode=2014PNAS..11112968L }}</ref> Later, {{ill|Diego Córdoba|eu|Diego Córdoba Gazolaz}} and {{ill|Luis Martínez-Zoroa|eu|Luis Martínez Zoroa}} introduced new approaches for constructing finite-time blowup singularities in a series of papers from 2023.<ref name="MMTPMWsz"/><ref>{{cite arXiv|last1=Córdoba|first1=Diego|last2=Martínez Zoroa|first2=Luis|title=Blow-up for the incompressible 3D-Euler equations with uniform $C^{1,\frac12-\varepsilon}\cap L^2$ force|date=15 September 2023|eprint=2309.08495|class=math.AP}}</ref> Ultimately, in collaboration with [[Fan Zheng]], they arrived at an unforced blowup result for 3D incompressible Euler equations<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Córdoba|first1=Diego|last2=Martínez-Zoroa|first2=Luis|last3=Zheng|first3=Fan|title=Finite time singularities to the 3D incompressible Euler equations for solutions in $C^\infty(\mathbb{R}^3\setminus\{0\})\cap C^{1,\alpha}\cap L^2$|journal=Annals of PDE|volume=11|number=2|year=2025|orig-date=23 August 2023|doi=10.1007/s40818-025-00214-2}}</ref> and a forced blowup result for so-called hypodissipative Navier–Stokes equations, a variant of the classical Navier–Stokes equations.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Córdoba|first1=Diego|last2=Martínez-Zoroa|first2=Luis|last3=Zheng|first3=Fan|title=Finite time blow-up for the hypodissipative Navier Stokes equations with a force in $L^1_t C_x^{1,\epsilon}\cap L^{\infty}_t L^2_x$|journal=[[Archive for Rational Mechanics and Analysis]]|volume=250|number=3|year=2026|orig-date=9 July 2024|page=38 |doi=10.1007/s00205-026-02198-0 |pmid=42131541 |pmc=13161257 }}</ref> Here, "unforced" means there is no external force present, and "forced" means the construction of such blowups revolves around deliberate choice of the external force. However, both results have gaps with the original Navier–Stokes problem, which excludes Euler equations and requires the external force to be smooth. Nonetheless, the two results together prompted beliefs that their strategy may be extended to the Millennium setup.<ref name="TTblog">{{cite web|last=Tao|first=Terence|author-link=Terence Tao|url=https://terrytao.wordpress.com/2026/09/07/finite-time-blowup-with-smooth-forcing-term-for-the-incompressible-porous-medium-boussinesq-and-incompressible-euler-equations|title=Finite time blowup with smooth forcing term for the incompressible porous medium, Boussinesq, and incompressible Euler equations|work=What's new|date=7 September 2026|access-date=9 September 2026}}</ref>

=== Buckmaster and Alpöge's collaboration ===
Tristan Buckmaster, professor of mathematics at the [[Courant Institute School of Mathematics, Computing, and Data Science|Courant Institute]], revealed in a statement on the night of 7 September 2026 shortly before midnight that he and [[Levent Alpöge]], a mathematician and an employee at the [[artificial intelligence]] company [[Anthropic]], had been trying to close the aforementioned gaps for at least a year in secrecy, employing several [[large language model]]s (LLMs) from both Anthropic and its immediate [[Competition in artificial intelligence|rival]]<ref name="RHverge"/> [[OpenAI]] in the research process.<ref name="CCft"/><ref name="TBstatement"/>{{rp|1}} Buckmaster and Alpöge each stressed that their work is "a strictly personal collaboration" and not associated with Anthropic in any formal or legal way, while Buckmaster mentioned he had a collaboration with [[Google DeepMind]].<ref name="CZACscience"/><ref name="TBstatement"/>{{rp|2}}<ref name="LAtweet">{{cite tweet|last=Alpöge|first=Levent|author-link=Levent Alpöge|user=__alpoge__|number=2097548261666033993|title=unfortunately i contacted them on the night of wednesday, september 2nd making the following points}}</ref> This collaboration presumably produced the preprint uploaded to [[arXiv]] on 17 September 2025 by 22 authors from academic institutions and DeepMind, including Buckmaster, demonstrating new numerical approaches to construct singularities of solutions to incompressible [[Porous medium|porous media]] (IPM) and [[Boussinesq approximation (buoyancy)|Boussinesq equations]], another two partial differential equations in fluid dynamics closely related to Navier–Stokes.<ref>{{cite arXiv|first1=Yongji|last1=Wang|first2=Mehdi|last2=Bennani|first3=James|last3=Martens|first4=Sébastien|last4=Racanière|first5=Sam|last5=Blackwell|first6=Alex|last6=Matthews|first7=Stanislav|last7=Nikolov|first8=Gonzalo|last8=Cao-Labora|first9=Daniel S.|last9=Park|first10=Martin|last10=Arjovsky|first11=Daniel|last11=Worrall|first12=Chongli|last12=Qin|first13=Ferran|last13=Alet|first14=Borislav|last14=Kozlovskii|first15=Nenad|last15=Tomašev|first16=Alex|last16=Davies|first17=Pushmeet|last17=Kohli|first18=Tristan|last18=Buckmaster|first19=Bogdan|last19=Georgiev|first20=Javier|last20=Gómez-Serrano|first21=Ray|last21=Jiang|first22=Ching-Yao|last22=Lai|title=Discovery of Unstable Singularities|eprint=2509.14185|date=17 September 2025|class=math.AP}}</ref> Two days later, on 19 September, Alpöge sent an email to Buckmaster expressing predictions that Navier–Stokes was the "only [...] Millennium Problem [that will be] solved in the foreseeable future" and concerns that "corporations [would] claim [...] the deepest pure math work", presumably initiating the year-long collaboration which is "in the traditional mathematical way".<ref name="GRusatoday"/><ref>{{cite tweet|last=Alpöge|first=Levent|author-link=Levent Alpöge|user=__alpoge__|number=2097206973418611054|title=Unfortunately this guy didn't title it ideal fluids explode}}</ref>

This collaboration eventually gave rise to smooth forcing results for Euler, IPM, and Boussinesq, reported together in the same post that contains the statement by Buckmaster,<ref name="TBmastodon"/> which were obtained on 15 August 2026 and verified a week later in [[Lean (proof assistant)|Lean]], an [[proof assistant|interactive theorem prover]] based on [[type theory]]. According to the statement, they originally intended to delay the announcement since they wanted to produce human-written and readable papers that are the result of their own understanding of the proofs.<ref name="CZACscience"/><ref name="TBstatement"/>{{rp|1}} Shortly after the post, mathematician [[Terence Tao]] congratulated the two in a blog post and on social media, calling the results "a remarkable achievement" and claiming "there does not seem to be anything in principle preventing the methods from extending all the way to Navier–Stokes".<ref name="TTblog"/><ref>{{cite web|last=Tao|first=Terence|author-link=Terence Tao|url=https://mathstodon.xyz/@tao/117233527638291447|title=A remarkable achievement|work=[[Mastodon (social network)|Mathstodon]]|date=8 September 2026|access-date=9 September 2026}}</ref> Buckmaster recognises the importance of the work of Córdoba and Martínez-Zoroa, saying the latter deserves a [[Fields Medal]], often considered the highest honour in mathematics.<ref name="TBstatement" />{{rp|1}}<ref name="MMTPMWsz"/> He left his office at 2:30 am on 8 September 2026.<ref name="KCnyt"/>

== Dispute between OpenAI and Buckmaster–Alpöge ==
=== OpenAI announcement ===
After an 88-hour run that started on 1 September 2026, an internal multiagent system of OpenAI produced a 166-page paper,<ref name="OAIpaper">{{cite web|author=OpenAI|author-link=OpenAI|url=https://cdn.openai.com/pdf/32d9f210-8b73-45e0-91bc-82a30aef8a9a/navier-stokes.pdf|date=8 September 2026|title=Finite time blowup for Navier–Stokes|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260908172948/https://cdn.openai.com/pdf/32d9f210-8b73-45e0-91bc-82a30aef8a9a/navier-stokes.pdf|archive-date=8 September 2026|access-date=9 September 2026}}</ref> along with a computer-verified Lean formalisation,<ref name="OAIpost">{{cite web|author=OpenAI|author-link=OpenAI|url=https://openai.com/index/navier-stokes-solution|title=On the Navier–Stokes Millennium Prize Problem|work=OpenAI|date=8 September 2026|access-date=9 September 2026|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260908171518/https://openai.com/index/navier-stokes-solution|archive-date=8 September 2026}}</ref> that are claimed to have established Fefferman's alternatives (C) and (D) in an announcement at noon on 8 September, approximately 12 hours after Buckmaster's post. At least 10,000 agents were employed, which, in the immediate process that led to the Navier–Stokes solution, sent 2.7 million messages and spent 130 billion output [[Large language model#Tokenization|tokens]].<ref name="OAIpost"/> It was estimated that the electricity cost alone would be in the order of millions,<ref>{{cite news|last=Metz|first=Cade|title=OpenAI Says It Has Cracked One of Math's 'Millennium Problems'|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/08/science/openai-proof-millennium-problem.html|work=[[The New York Times]]|date=8 September 2026|access-date=9 September 2026}}</ref><ref name="KHbbc"/><ref>{{cite magazine|last=Sparkes|first=Matthew|url=https://www.newscientist.com/article/2588063-openai-has-solved-the-navier-stokes-millennium-problem-using-15m-of-ai-effort|title=OpenAI has solved the Navier-Stokes Millennium problem using $15m of AI effort|magazine=[[New Scientist]]|date=8 September 2026|access-date=10 September 2026}}</ref><ref name="JKfortune"/> which was confirmed by OpenAI researcher [[Noam Brown]].<ref>{{cite tweet|last=Brown|first=Noam|user=polynoamial|number=2097375837670785447|title=Yes, this result cost millions of dollars}}</ref>

OpenAI acknowledged that Buckmaster and Alpöge's input to models of OpenAI via their use of [[OpenAI Codex (AI agent)|Codex]] might have improved the model used for the run, whose training started on 28 August;<ref name="OAIpost"/> on the same date, Brown said that OpenAI had already attempted Millennium Prize Problems but failed to produce any result.<ref>{{cite tweet|last=Brown|first=Noam|user=polynoamial|number=2093460474738393511|title=We already did, it didn't solve any of them}}</ref> OpenAI explained that it was rumours about two Millennium problems being solved that motivated them to initiate an attempt at all six open problems using the model,<ref name="OAIpost"/> with OpenAI researcher [[Sébastien Bubeck]] later further specifying that the rumours explicitly mentioned Anthropic resolved the two and were started by "viral [tweets]".<ref name="SBtweet"/><ref name="ACconvo"/> It is not clear which tweets he is referring to, but Alpöge's tweet "Augustus Mirabilis" (miraculous August) on 31 August<ref>{{cite tweet|last=Alpöge|first=Levent|author-link=Levent Alpöge|user=__alpoge__|number=2094598608704111101|title=Augustus Mirabilis}}</ref> was cited as what led OpenAI to believe that, by extension, Anthropic had solved at least one Millennium problem.<ref name="SBtweet2">{{cite tweet|last=Bubeck|first=Sébastien|author-link=Sébastien Bubeck|user=SebastienBubeck|number=2097379415747342689|title=Some more technical points}}</ref> OpenAI further explained that they "later realized" the rumours were related to Alpöge and Buckmaster.<ref name="OAIpost"/><ref name="DCnature">{{cite journal|last=Castelvecchi|first=Davide|title=OpenAI claims huge maths breakthrough on a famed 'Millennium Problem'|journal=[[Nature (journal)|Nature]]|date=8 September 2026|volume=657 |issue=8132 |pages=579–580 |doi=10.1038/d41586-026-02842-5}}</ref>

=== Buckmaster and Alpöge's contact with OpenAI before the announcement ===
According to both Buckmaster's statement and Alpöge's tweet the next day on 9 September,<ref name="LAtweet"/> Alpöge received tips that his work with Buckmaster had been leaked to OpenAI. Prompted by this, the two mathematicians contacted OpenAI independently—Alpöge on the night of 2 September, and Buckmaster on 3 September (to an unnamed mathematician at OpenAI), expressing his confidence in potential advances on Navier–Stokes and his wishes against rushing an AI write-up and a Lean certificate. He was then later contacted by Bubeck, who insisted on meeting with him as soon as possible, still under the impression that Buckmaster and Alpöge had resolved Navier–Stokes instead of smooth forced Euler.<ref name="SBtweet"/><ref name="TBstatement" />{{rp|2}} Bubeck contacted both again on 6 September, first messaging Alpöge at 11:48 about OpenAI's resolution of Navier–Stokes which used "very little human input" and that they were "ready to share everything [...] including the human prompts" since he wanted "to be maximally open", and then later at 12:45 asking Buckmaster if they could meet "at any point today".<ref name="OAIpost"/><ref name="SBtweet"/><ref name="TBstatement" />{{rp|2}}

A meeting was held later in the afternoon between Buckmaster, Bubeck and the unnamed mathematician; Alpöge did not attend.<ref name="TBstatement" />{{rp|2}} Buckmaster, being told some more details about OpenAI's solution, made mathematical judgements that led him to the conclusion that OpenAI did pursue the path he and Alpöge had been working on, namely the Córdoba–Martínez-Zoroa programme.<ref name="ACconvo"/><ref name="TBstatement" />{{rp|3}} He also learned that a large team within OpenAI had been working on the problem and initially tried easier problems, including ones concerning Euler equations; he interpreted this as contradicting the "very little human input" Bubeck earlier told Alpöge,<ref name="TBstatement" />{{rp|3}} but Bubeck later explained that this meant the team did not contain experts in Navier–Stokes-related fields and hence there was no one from the team who could "meaningfully contribute to the mathematical content".<ref name="SBtweet2"/> Buckmaster then asked if OpenAI had direct access to files that he and Alpöge had input into Codex, including entire drafts of papers, or if OpenAI used sessions to train their models.<ref name="MMaxios"/> OpenAI rejected the first during the meeting but admitted the second in the later post, albeit in a downplaying manner, saying that the data are "de-identified" and "derived" from their use.<ref name="OAIpost"/><ref name="CCft"/>

OpenAI then proposed to Buckmaster that he first reports their Euler result before OpenAI announces their Navier–Stokes result, or, if he is willing, that he rewrites OpenAI's proof on behalf of the company, either as the sole author (per Buckmaster) or lead author (per Bubeck); but in any case the prize pledged by the Clay Mathematics Institute for a correct solution to a Millennium problem, one million [[United States dollar|US dollars]], belongs to Buckmaster and Alpöge as they are the "closest humans to the problem".<ref name="DMJBabc">{{cite news|last1=Maguire|first1=Dannielle|last2=Bowler|first2=Jacinta|url=https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-09-10/openai-navier-stokes-millennium-problem-claims/107132242|title=Controversy erupts as OpenAI claims solution to Navier Stokes maths problem|work=[[ABC News (Australia)|ABC News]]|date=10 September 2026|access-date=10 September 2026}}</ref><ref name="JKfortune"/><ref name="TBstatement" />{{rp|3}} In the second proposal, both Buckmaster and Bubeck confirmed that the latter asserted against Alpöge being listed as author of the human-rewritten paper, citing [[conflict of interest]].<ref name="TBstatement" />{{rp|3}}<ref name="SBtweet"/> Buckmaster declined both offers, rejecting that he (in the first proposal) or Alpöge (in the second) be removed from authorship of work initiated by them.<ref name="GRusatoday">{{cite news|last=Reich|first=Greta|url=https://eu.usatoday.com/story/tech/2026/09/08/openai-navier-stokes-breakthrough/91664870007|title=OpenAI touts math breakthrough. Mathematicians dispute credit|work=[[USA Today]]|date=8 September 2026|access-date=9 September 2026}}</ref> He pushed further that if OpenAI went ahead and announced their proof, he would make the dispute public;<ref name="RBtc"/> to which Bubeck asked why one would risk to ruin their career over "unfounded accusations".<ref name="MFtelegraph"/><ref name="SBtweet"/><ref name="TBstatement" />{{rp|3}} Buckmaster in turn understood this as a threat,<ref name="MFtelegraph">{{cite news|last=Field|first=Matthew|url=https://www.telegraph.co.uk/business/2026/09/08/openai-accused-of-exploiting-and-threatening-mathematician|title=OpenAI accused of threatening professor in race to crack 90-year-old maths puzzle|work=[[The Daily Telegraph|The Telegraph]]|date=8 September 2026|access-date=9 September 2026}}</ref> responded with confusion as to why going public would be career suicide and claimed to have received the reply "if you don't want me to be nice, then I don't have to be nice."<ref name="RHverge"/> Bubeck apologised for his choice of words in his tweet after the OpenAI announcement.<ref name="MMTPMWsz">{{cite news|last1=Muth|first1=Max|last2=Palm|first2=Theresa|last3=Weiß|first3=Marlene|url=https://www.sueddeutsche.de/wissen/openai-navier-stokes-problem-streit-li.3544733|title=Open AI will ein Millennium-Problem gelöst haben|language=de|work=[[Süddeutsche Zeitung]]|date=9 September 2026|access-date=10 September 2026}}</ref><ref name="SBtweet"/>

=== Timeline of OpenAI assertions concerning reuse of user data ===
* 8 September morning, initial press release: "We (the researchers and the agents) did not see any of their work through any means until they released it publicly — in particular, no specific user data was accessed in order to solve this problem. While unlikely, we cannot rule out that de-identified data derived from their usage of our products helped improve our models⁠."<ref name="OAIpost"/>
* 8 September morning, chief research officer Mark Chen: "No people or AI systems searched through user data to solve this problem or any specific problem that we were trying. And I'm a little bit disappointed by the allegations of the huge breach of user trust. We did not do that."<ref name="CFvb">{{cite news|last=Franzen|first=Carl|url=https://venturebeat.com/technology/openai-solves-longstanding-math-problem-with-10-000-agent-swarm-but-cant-rule-out-benefitting-from-a-researchers-private-codex-data|title=OpenAI solves longstanding math problem with 10,000-agent swarm — but can't rule out benefitting from a researcher's private Codex data|work=[[VentureBeat]]|date=8 September 2026|access-date=13 September 2026}}</ref>
* 8 September afternoon, official tweet: "We (the researchers and the agents) did not see any of their work through any means until they released it publicly — in particular, no specific user data was accessed in order to solve this problem. While unlikely, we cannot rule out that de-identified data derived from their usage of our products helped improve our models. However, our proofs differ significantly and even the precise results proved are different in the Euler case (forced vs. unforced)."<ref>{{cite tweet|user=OpenAI|number=2097375276384567642|title=We congratulate Levent Alpöge and Tristan Buckmaster on their remarkable mathematical work}}</ref>
* 9 September evening, spokesperson Laurance Fauconnet: "We can say categorically that it is impossible for Dr. Buckmaster's Codex prompts over the last two months to have influenced the system in any way, including training."<ref name="KCnyt"/><ref name="RHverge2"/>
* 10 September late evening, updated press release: "Following an investigation, we have confirmed that Buckmaster's Codex prompts over the two months preceding this announcement and paper on September 8, 2026, could not have influenced the system in any way, including through training. The OpenAI internal model used for this result was developed through large-scale reinforcement learning on top of a previously pretrained model."<ref name="OAIpost"/>
* 13 September, Fauconnet: "After investigating, we can say with full confidence that no user inputs past July 3rd could have influenced this system in any way."<ref>{{cite news|last=Waldvogel|first=Miriam|url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/technology/2026/09/13/he-was-close-1-million-breakthrough-then-openai-swooped|title=He was close to a huge math breakthrough. Then he got scooped by AI.|newspaper=[[The Washington Post]]|date=13 September 2026|access-date=18 September 2026}}</ref>

== Further responses ==
{{see also|Competition in artificial intelligence}}
=== People associated with the two parties ===
After OpenAI's announcement, Buckmaster explicitly accused them on social media of "us[ing] customer's data to try to scoop their customer", citing OpenAI's admission to using user data for model training.<ref>{{cite web|last=Buckmaster|first=Tristan|url=https://mastodon.social/@tristanbuckmaster/117236471352470303|title="Since August 28 we have been training..."|work=[[Mastodon (social network)|Mastodon]]|date=8 September 2026|access-date=9 September 2026}}</ref> Alpöge made the same accusation more implicitly in a tweet approximately one hour later.<ref name="LAtweet2">{{cite tweet|last=Alpöge|first=Levent|author-link=Levent Alpöge|user=__alpoge__|number=2097383870773748190|title="we cannot rule out that de-identified data..."}}</ref><ref name="CCft">{{cite news|last=Criddle|first=Cristina|url=https://www.ft.com/content/4d6d28a0-4b12-438e-8850-4b3d49fc57f5?syn-25a6b1a6=1|title=OpenAI faces competing claims around maths breakthrough|work=[[Financial Times]]|date=9 September 2026|access-date=10 September 2026|url-access=subscription}}</ref> Buckmaster also criticised an earlier version of OpenAI's paper for having no references to the work of Córdoba and Martínez-Zoroa, which were later added in a new 166-page version.<ref>{{cite web|last=Buckmaster|first=Tristan|url=https://mastodon.social/@tristanbuckmaster/117237555794407063|title=Just to point something out to Open AI|work=[[Mastodon (social network)|Mastodon]]|date=8 September 2026|access-date=9 September 2026}}</ref><ref name="OAIpaper"/> Professor at the [[University of Erlangen–Nuremberg]] Emil Wiedemann also pointed out that a longer list of references was expected for such a "monumental proof".<ref name="MMTPMWsz"/>

Bubeck called the meeting with Buckmaster "incredibly difficult".<ref name="SBtweet"/> [[Sam Altman]], CEO of OpenAI, retweeted Bubeck's statement and maintained that OpenAI has contacted Buckmaster and Alpöge in [[good faith]].<ref name="KNindiatoday"/> He emphasised that the methods of Buckmaster and Alpöge's work and of OpenAI's solution "appear to be different" and hence the two are independent<ref name="SAtweet"/>—so did Ven Chandrasekaran, a mathematician at the company<ref>{{cite magazine|last1=Knight|first1=Will|last2=Zeff|first2=Maxwell|url=https://www.wired.com/story/openai-navier-stokes-math-discovery-academics|title=OpenAI Just Claimed a Huge Math Discovery. Some Academics Are Crying Foul|magazine=[[Wired (magazine)|Wired]]|date=8 September 2026|access-date=10 September 2026}}</ref>—but Alpöge refuted this argument, saying OpenAI's proof "looks more along the lines of another Euler blowup proof we had". Alpöge also expressed disappointment in OpenAI's unwillingness to include him in the potential human-rewritten paper of OpenAI's solution and in their offering of the Millennium Prize, and ultimately in the failure of two AI labs to cooperate on science.<ref name="LAtweet2"/> A colleague at Anthropic, Sholto Douglas, shared the latter sentiment<ref>{{cite tweet|last=Douglas|first=Sholto|user=_sholtodouglas|number=2097224624274911368|title=It is extremely sad that this didn't end up as an example of how the labs could cooperate}}</ref> and offered sympathy in Buckmaster and Alpöge not being able to bridge their gaps to Navier–Stokes in the way they intended.<ref>{{cite tweet|last=Douglas|first=Sholto|user=_sholtodouglas|number=2097218331690578000|title=levent is a really sweet guy with great intentions}}</ref> Mark Chen, chief research officer of OpenAI, reiterated that "no people or AI systems searched through user data to solve this problem".<ref name="MMaxios"/>

In a recounting of the events on the afternoon of 8 September, Buckmaster asserted that he did not have an interest in the prize money or even winning the race to the answer per se; he simply wished himself and Alpöge to be credited since they were "part of the [mathematical] story". He called the intention of OpenAI to remove Alpöge's authorship "the big sticking point", and considered himself to be an innocent bystander of the "petty games" or childish "petty drama"<ref name="RHverge2"/> that is the rivalry between OpenAI and Anthropic, with the former on the evening of 9 September going further in their denying of using Buckmaster's Codex prompts, calling it "categorically impossible".<ref name="KCnyt">{{cite news|last=Chang|first=Kenneth|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/10/science/tristan-buckmaster-openai-math-navier-stokes.html|title=An N.Y.U. Mathematician Clashed With OpenAI Over a $1 Million Proof|work=[[The New York Times]]|date=10 September 2026|access-date=11 September 2026}}</ref> On the general issue of changes to mathematics brought about by AI, Buckmaster considers the race for more papers and credit now "pointless" and calls for discussion within the mathematical community to re-evaluate the nature of the discipline<ref>{{cite news|last=Wilson|first=Cam|url=https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-09-11/racing-to-solve-maths-problems-pointless-tristan-buckmaster-says/107141628|title=Racing to solve maths problems now 'pointless', says Australian at centre of OpenAI controversy|work=[[ABC News (Australia)|ABC News]]|date=11 September 2026|access-date=11 September 2026}}</ref> and operational aspects including credit assignment and hiring.<ref>{{cite news|last=Gardner|first=Jessica|url=https://www.afr.com/world/north-america/not-selling-my-soul-why-this-aussie-maths-professor-took-on-openai-20260911-p60wf8|title='Not selling my soul': Why this Aussie maths professor took on OpenAI|work=[[Australian Financial Review]]|date=11 September 2026|access-date=11 September 2026}}</ref>

=== Wider public ===
[[Terence Tao]] raised general concerns on his social media about the future of mathematical collaboration between humans; he worried that rumours about a mathematician's own work might prompt AI companies to invest huge efforts into pushing it instead of allowing the mathematician to develop their research to "full potential", whether the companies know about the details of the human mathematician's work or not.<ref>{{cite web|last=Tao|first=Terence|author-link=Terence Tao|url=https://mathstodon.xyz/@tao/117237322160500501|title=However, one notable feature of the current AI era|work=[[Mastodon (social network)|Mathstodon]]|date=8 September 2026|access-date=9 September 2026}}</ref> He also expressed dissatisfaction with the current conduct of AI companies "using press releases or social media posts to communicate mathematical results" instead of uploading preprints or arranging talks at conferences,<ref name="DCnature"/> not taking the mathematical obligation to push broader understanding of their results.<ref name="ACconvo">{{cite web|last=Cullen|first=Andrew|url=https://theconversation.com/openai-claims-another-huge-mathematical-result-amid-fights-over-credit-ethics-and-privacy-291575|title=OpenAI claims another huge mathematical result amid fights over credit, ethics and privacy|work=[[The Conversation (website)|The Conversation]]|date=10 September 2026|access-date=10 September 2026}}</ref> Mathematician [[Michael Harris (mathematician)|Michael Harris]] however said such high-level financial investments would not continue as "there is no profit in it"; however, he also worries that practices of AI companies related to mathematics would "convince decision makers that human mathematicians are obsolete, and [...] young people that their passion for mathematics has no future", hence "extremely damaging to mathematics".<ref name="CZACscience"/> Professor at [[Queen Mary University of London]] Abhishek Saha agreed that there are few other such "high-caliber" problems that AI companies are willing to invest "such vast sums solving".<ref name="RHverge">{{cite news|last=Hart|first=Robert|url=https://www.theverge.com/ai-artificial-intelligence/992953/openai-math-millennium-prize-navier-stokes|title=OpenAI's sly mathematical breakthrough sends a chill through academia|work=[[The Verge]]|date=9 September 2026|access-date=10 September 2026}}</ref> Professor at [[Leibniz University Hannover]] {{ill|Joachim Escher|de|Joachim Escher (Mathematiker)}} said asking every mathematical problem to OpenAI was simply impossible due to energy and capacity constraints, hence mathematics had not "reached its end".<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.srf.ch/news/international/millennium-problem-geloest-ki-loest-uraltes-mathematik-raetsel-was-das-bedeutet|title=KI löst uraltes Mathematik-Rätsel – was das bedeutet|language=de-CH|work=[[Schweizer Radio und Fernsehen]]|date=9 September 2026|access-date=10 September 2026}}</ref> On the other hand, Wiedemann worries that mathematics will no longer be a competition between intelligence and diligence, but material resources.<ref name="MMTPMWsz"/> Mathematician [[Shing-Tung Yau]] also raised concerns that the disparity of resources held between AI companies and early career researchers could discourage the latter "to pursue ambitious questions".<ref name="RHverge2"/>

Although [[Martin Bridson]], president of the Clay Mathematics Institute, called the series of announcements "exciting", he stressed that the Institute requires a solution to a Millennium problem to be in the form of peer-reviewed publications, which would then be further scrutinised before the prize is awarded.<ref name="DCnature"/> Later on 11 September, the Institute released a statement acknowledging that "the Navier–Stokes problem has apparently been settled" but maintained the process for verification and credit assignment "is deliberately unhurried";<ref>{{cite web|author=Clay Mathematics Institute|author-link=Clay Mathematics Institute|url=https://www.claymath.org/news/navier-stokes-announcement|title=Navier–Stokes Announcement|work=Clay Mathematics Institute|date=11 September 2026|access-date=13 September 2026}}</ref> the status of the Navier–Stokes problem is now "active" instead of unsolved or solved on the Institute's website.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.claymath.org/millennium-problems|title=The Millennium Prize Problems|work=Clay Mathematics Institute|access-date=13 September 2026}}</ref> Meanwhile, [[Ravi Vakil]] and John Meier, on behalf of the [[American Mathematical Society]], congratulated both Alpöge–Buckmaster and OpenAI for "a milestone advance in human knowledge".<ref>{{cite news|last1=Vakil|first1=Ravi|last2=Meier|first2=John|author-link1=Ravi Vakil|url=https://www.ams.org/news?news_id=7686|title=Statement from AMS Leadership on Navier–Stokes Problem|work=[[American Mathematical Society|AMS Newsroom]]|date=8 September 2026|access-date=10 September 2026}}</ref>

Joseph Perla, founder of model-routing company TrustedRouter, staunchly stands against OpenAI's decision and way of announcing their solution, saying "this is what all the labs do every day: read your chats and copy ideas".<ref name="MMaxios"/> Mathematician [[Andreas Thom (mathematician)|Andreas Thom]] also pointed to the general "unanswered question" of lack of transparency between OpenAI and mathematicians, suggesting that models of the former have been "hoovering up unpublished human work and presenting it as AI generated".<ref>{{cite web|last=Thom|first=Andreas|author-link=Andreas Thom (mathematician)|url=https://mathstodon.xyz/@andreasthom/117240535270608201|title=I want to record a number of points that I realized after reading up on the controversy|work=[[Mastodon (social network)|Mathstodon]]|date=9 September 2026|access-date=10 September 2026}}</ref><ref name="ACconvo"/> Lecturer at [[Monash University]] Melissa Lee raised similar concerns and warned researchers "to know very clearly what happens to unpublished work they enter into AI systems".<ref name="DMJBabc"/>

Professor at the [[University of Sydney]] Zsuzsanna Dancso accused OpenAI of failing to observe two fundamental ethics in science: "one is we acknowledge our sources, and two is we acknowledge our collaborators".<ref name="DMJBabc"/> Mathematician [[Peter Sarnak]] commended Buckmaster for "behaving the way mathematicians behave",<ref name="KCnyt"/> while Alpöge previously also called him "a mathematician's mathematician" and praised him for his integrity.<ref name="LAtweet"/> Martínez-Zoroa thanked Buckmaster for crediting him and Córdoba and "mak[ing] it clear that the ideas came from [their] group".<ref name="PFdLpais"/> Córdoba, initially in shock about the news and having been notified by neither of the two parties, acknowledged the current tendency to incorporate AI in mathematical research, but considered human-written proofs still essential and AI unable to find new original ideas in the foreseeable future; he stressed that "if [their] work had not existed, AI would not have solved the problem".<ref name="PFdLpais">{{cite news|last=Fernández de Lis|first=Patricia|url=https://elpais.com/ciencia/2026-09-10/un-ano-de-trabajo-de-dos-matematicos-espanoles-frente-a-88-horas-y-15-millones-de-openai-sin-nuestra-idea-la-ia-no-lo-habria-resuelto.html|title=Un año de trabajo de dos matemáticos españoles frente a 88 horas y 15 millones de OpenAI: "Sin nuestra idea, la IA no lo habría resuelto"|language=es|work=[[El País]]|date=10 September 2026|access-date=11 September 2026}}</ref> Mathematician [[Steven Strogatz]] called Buckmaster "a real gentleman" and wished the Millennium prize money to go to Córdoba and Martínez-Zoroa; however, he feared that machines could learn and be skilled in even aspects of mathematics that are perceived as intrinsically human, including interpretation and communication for advancing human understanding, or appreciation and arbitration of aesthetic values in mathematical work.<ref>{{cite magazine|last=Ward|first=Isabella|url=https://www.wired.com/story/mathematician-steven-strogatz-grapples-with-ai-recent-breakthroughs|title='I'm Really Terrified': A Mathematician Grapples With AI's Recent Breakthroughs|magazine=[[Wired (magazine)|Wired]]|date=12 September 2026|access-date=13 September 2026}}</ref>

On 11 September 2026, 24 [[Fields Medal|Fields Medalists]] (later cosigned by two more) published an open letter titled ''A Severe Misalignment of AI in Mathematics'', warning that the human foundation of interaction and student nurture and the core value of "conceptual understanding and insight" that form a "fertile ground" for mathematics could be eroded by the failure to hinder AI companies from continuing the "push" to resolve mathematical problems en masse.<ref name="fieldsOpenLetter"/> Such concerns have been put in the larger context of [[Cognitive load|cognitive offloading]] and the possibility of humans becoming more reliant on AI tools for information processing and [[critical thinking]].<ref name="economist11"/>
